results.name: above_vs_below_span_asymmetry
results.description: Yes rate for targets 1-15 above the set max minus yes rate for targets 1-15 below the set min; model intervals are width-only (symmetric), so observed != null_mean shows a directional (upward vs downward) generalization bias the model misses.
results.code:
# name: above_vs_below_span_asymmetry
# description: Yes rate for targets 1-15 above the set max minus yes rate for targets 1-15 below the set min; model intervals are width-only (symmetric), so observed != null_mean shows a directional (upward vs downward) generalization bias the model misses.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(s, axis=1); mx = np.nanmax(s, axis=1)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(s), axis=1)
    up = (t > mx) & (t - mx <= 15)
    dn = (t < mn) & (mn - t <= 15)
    if not up.any() or not dn.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[up].mean() - r[dn].mean())

results.name: wide_span_interior_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets strictly inside the examples range when the range is >=40 wide; observed below null_mean means the model over-fills wide spans with interval hypotheses (people treat sparse wide sets as rule-like, not as ranges).
results.code:
# name: wide_span_interior_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets strictly inside the examples range when the range is >=40 wide; observed below null_mean means the model over-fills wide spans with interval hypotheses (people treat sparse wide sets as rule-like, not as ranges).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(s, axis=1); mx = np.nanmax(s, axis=1)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(s), axis=1)
    notin = ~np.any(s == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = notin & (t > mn) & (t < mx) & ((mx - mn) >= 40) & (n >= 2)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: near_span_decay_slope
results.description: Among targets outside the examples range and within 40 of it, OLS slope of yes on distance-to-range (per 10 units); observed less negative than null_mean means people generalize to nearby numbers more gradually (flatter) than the model, more negative means a sharper fall-off.
results.code:
# name: near_span_decay_slope
# description: Among targets outside the examples range and within 40 of it, OLS slope of yes on distance-to-range (per 10 units); observed less negative than null_mean means people generalize to nearby numbers more gradually (flatter) than the model, more negative means a sharper fall-off.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(s, axis=1); mx = np.nanmax(s, axis=1)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(s), axis=1)
    dist = np.where(t > mx, t - mx, np.where(t < mn, mn - t, 0.0))
    m = (dist > 0) & (dist <= 40)
    if m.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x = dist[m] / 10.0; y = r[m]
    x = x - x.mean(); v = (x * x).sum()
    return float((x * (y - y.mean())).sum() / v) if v > 0 else 0.0

results.name: trial_index_yes_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes response on trial_index (per 100 trials); model has no time dependence, so a nonzero observed slope vs null_mean ~0 indicates drift in yes-bias over the session.
results.code:
# name: trial_index_yes_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes response on trial_index (per 100 trials); model has no time dependence, so a nonzero observed slope vs null_mean ~0 indicates drift in yes-bias over the session.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(s, axis=1); mx = np.nanmax(s, axis=1)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(s), axis=1)
    x = df["trial_index"].astype(float).to_numpy() / 100.0
    x = x - x.mean()
    v = (x * x).sum()
    return float((x * (r - r.mean())).sum() / v) if v > 0 else 0.0

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: Among multi-example sets, targets not in set and within 15 of exactly one of the first/last example: yes rate (near last shown) minus yes rate (near first shown); model is order-invariant, so observed > null_mean means recency-weighted generalization.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: Among multi-example sets, targets not in set and within 15 of exactly one of the first/last example: yes rate (near last shown) minus yes rate (near first shown); model is order-invariant, so observed > null_mean means recency-weighted generalization.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(s, axis=1); mx = np.nanmax(s, axis=1)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(s), axis=1)
    idx_last = n - 1
    first = s[:, 0]
    last = s[np.arange(len(s)), idx_last]
    dfst = np.abs(t - first); dlst = np.abs(t - last)
    notin = ~np.any(s == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & notin & (np.abs(first - last) > 30)
    nl = base & (dlst <= 15) & (dfst > 15)
    nf = base & (dfst <= 15) & (dlst > 15)
    if not nl.any() or not nf.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[nl].mean() - r[nf].mean())

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets at least 30 away from every shown example; the model has no lapse/guessing term, so observed above null_mean means people say yes to distant targets more than the model allows.
results.code:
# name: far_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets at least 30 away from every shown example; the model has no lapse/guessing term, so observed above null_mean means people say yes to distant targets more than the model allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(s, axis=1); mx = np.nanmax(s, axis=1)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(s), axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(s - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = d >= 30
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: For sets whose examples all share one parity, among non-example targets within the examples range +/-10: yes rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null_mean means people use parity more than the model, < means less.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: For sets whose examples all share one parity, among non-example targets within the examples range +/-10: yes rate for same-parity targets minus opposite-parity targets; observed > null_mean means people use parity more than the model, < means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(s, axis=1); mx = np.nanmax(s, axis=1)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(s), axis=1)
    par = np.mod(s, 2)
    allsame = (np.nanmax(par, axis=1) == np.nanmin(par, axis=1)) & (n >= 2)
    notin = ~np.any(s == t[:, None], axis=1)
    near = (t >= mn - 10) & (t <= mx + 10)
    same = np.mod(t, 2) == par[:, 0]
    base = allsame & notin & near
    a = base & same; b = base & ~same
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
